LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundations of Gastroi:
Overview — GI Motility
GI motility = the coordinated muscular movement that propels food through the gut and mixes it with secretions — from swallowing to defecation.
The organising principle: the gut has its own nervous system (the enteric nervous system) that runs motility semi-autonomously, modulated by the autonomic system and gut hormones — and each region has a specialised movement pattern for its job (propulsion vs mixing vs storage).
Why it matters: explains dysphagia/achalasia, gastroparesis, ileus, constipation, Hirschsprung's, and how prokinetics/anti-motility drugs work — cross-ref the autonomic nervous system, GI secretions, bowel obstruction/ileus, clinical GI notes.
The Gut Wall & Its Muscle
  • Motility comes from the muscularis externa: an inner circular + outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer, with the myenteric plexus between them
  • Smooth muscle behaves as a syncytium (cells electrically coupled) → coordinated contraction
The Control Systems — three layers of control
System Role

The ENS point (high-yield): the gut can run motility independently of the CNS (the ENS has more neurons than the spinal cord) — the brain modulates but doesn't generate the basic patterns.
Interstitial cells of Cajal: generate slow waves (the basal electrical rhythm) that set the pace of contractions.

  • Defecation reflex: rectal stretch → internal sphincter relaxes (involuntary) + external sphincter voluntary control
  • The sphincters: LOS, pyloric, ileocaecal, internal + external anal — each gates flow between segments

Overview — GI Secretions
The GI tract secretes ~7 L of fluid daily — enzymes, acid, bicarbonate, bile, and mucus — to digest food, protect the mucosa, and create the right environment for each digestive step.
The organising principle: each region secretes something specific for its job, controlled by a mix of neural (vagal), hormonal (gastrin, CCK, secretin), and local signals — and the three phases of digestion (cephalic, gastric, intestinal) time these secretions to the meal.
Why it matters: explains peptic ulcers + PPIs/H2 blockers, pancreatic insufficiency, the secretions lost in vomiting/diarrhoea/fistulae, and pernicious anaemia (intrinsic factor) — cross-ref GI motility, digestion/absorption, gut hormones, peptic ulcer disease, clinical GI notes.

  • Also the route for bilirubin excretion (cross-ref bilirubin metabolism)

Overview — Digestion & Absorption of Macronutrients
Digestion breaks the three macronutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats — into absorbable units, which are then taken up across the small intestine (the absorptive organ).
The organising principle: each macronutrient has its own enzyme sequence → final absorbable unit → transport mechanism, and most absorption happens in the small intestine (hugely amplified surface area). Fat is the odd one out (needs bile + a lymphatic route).
Why it matters: explains coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, lactose intolerance, bile-salt/fat malabsorption, B12/iron/folate absorption, and steatorrhoea — cross-ref GI secretions (the enzymes), coeliac, pancreatic insufficiency, clinical GI notes.
The Absorptive Surface — why the small intestine
  • Built for absorption: circular folds → villi → microvilli (brush border) → enormously amplified surface area
  • The brush border carries the final digestive enzymes (disaccharidases, peptidases) → digestion is completed at the absorptive surface
  • The coeliac link: villous atrophy (coeliac) → loss of surface area → malabsorption
Carbohydrate Digestion & Absorption
Digestion
  • Salivary + pancreatic amylase break starch → disaccharides (maltose) + oligosaccharides
  • Brush-border disaccharidases (maltase, lactase, sucrase) → monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose)
Absorption (only monosaccharides)
  • Glucose + galactose: SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled, active) into the enterocyte
  • Fructose: GLUT5 (facilitated)
  • Then GLUT2 out into the blood
The lactose intolerance link (high-yield): lactase deficiency → undigested lactose → osmotic diarrhoea + bacterial fermentation (bloating, wind).
Protein Digestion & Absorption
Digestion
  • Stomach: pepsin (from pepsinogen, in acid) begins protein breakdown
  • Pancreas: proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin — activated from zymogens in the duodenum) → peptides
  • Brush-border peptidases → amino acids + di/tripeptides
  • Absorption: amino acids via Na⁺-coupled transporters; di/tripeptides via PepT1 (H⁺-coupled) → broken down to amino acids inside the enterocyte → into blood
  • The pancreas does the bulk of protein digestion → pancreatic insufficiency → protein (+ fat) malabsorption
Fat Digestion & Absorption — the odd one out (high-yield)
Fat is hydrophobic, so it needs special handling (bile + a lymphatic route):
  • Emulsification: bile salts (liver/gallbladder, CCK-released) break fat globules into small droplets → ↑surface area
  • Digestion: pancreatic lipase → monoglycerides + free fatty acids
  • Micelle formation: bile salts package these into micelles → ferry them to the brush border
  • Absorption: fatty acids/monoglycerides diffuse into the enterocyte → re-esterified into triglycerides → packaged into chylomicrons
The lymphatic route (the key difference): chylomicrons are too big for capillaries → enter the lymphatics (lacteals) → thoracic duct → blood (whereas carbs/proteins go straight into the portal blood).
Fat-soluble vitamins: ADEK are absorbed with fat (in micelles) → fat malabsorption → ADEK deficiency.
The malabsorption links (high-yield): anything disrupting this → steatorrhoea (fatty, pale, floating, offensive stool):
  • ↓bile (obstruction, cholestasis, bile-salt malabsorption) → can't emulsify
  • ↓lipase (pancreatic insufficiency, CF) → can't digest
  • ↓surface (coeliac, Crohn's) → can't absorb

Overview — Gut Hormones
The gut is the largest endocrine organ in the body — scattered enteroendocrine cells in the mucosa release hormones that coordinate digestion, secretion, motility, and appetite.
The organising principle: food in the gut lumen → stimulates a specific cell → releases a hormone → that hormone prepares the next part of the GI tract for what's coming (feed-forward control). Most act in a logical pairing (the stimulus and the response make physiological sense).
Why it matters: explains Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, the incretin effect (GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors in T2DM), octreotide (somatostatin), carcinoid, and appetite/obesity physiology — cross-ref GI secretions, peptic ulcer disease, diabetes pharmacology.

The Hormones in Detail
Gastrin — the acid driver
  • From G cells in the antrum → drives parietal cell acid secretion (directly + via histamine from ECL cells) and stimulates mucosal growth
  • Inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and somatostatin
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (high-yield): a gastrinoma (gastrin-secreting tumour, often pancreatic/duodenal) → unregulated acid → multiple/refractory peptic ulcers (incl. atypical sites), diarrhoea. Think of it with recurrent ulcers despite PPI / ulcers in odd places.
CCK & Secretin — the duodenal pair (the logic)
  • CCK responds to fat + protein → contracts the gallbladder (delivers bile to emulsify fat) + releases pancreatic enzymes (to digest it) + signals satiety + slows gastric emptying (so the duodenum isn't overwhelmed)
  • Secretin responds to acid → releases bicarbonate from pancreas/bile ducts (to neutralise the acid so pancreatic enzymes can work) + turns down gastric acid
The pairing logic: fat/protein arrive → CCK brings the tools to digest them; acid arrives → secretin brings the buffer to neutralise it. The stimulus always predicts the response.
Incretins — GIP & GLP-1 (the diabetes link)
  • The incretin effect: oral glucose triggers more insulin than the same glucose given IV — because the gut releases GIP + GLP-1, which prime the pancreas before glucose even hits the blood (feed-forward)
  • GLP-1 also: ↓ glucagon, slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety → weight loss
  • Both are rapidly broken down by DPP-4
Pharmacology payoff (T2DM): GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide — resist DPP-4) → ↑insulin, satiety, weight loss; DPP-4 inhibitors ("gliptins", e.g. sitagliptin) → block breakdown → ↑ endogenous incretins. Glucose-dependent action → low hypo risk.

Overview — Liver Function & Metabolism
The liver is the body's central metabolic and detoxifying organ — it processes everything absorbed from the gut (via the portal vein), synthesises key proteins, stores nutrients, metabolises drugs, and excretes waste.
The organising principle: the liver has a handful of core functions — metabolism, synthesis, storage, detoxification, and excretion — and liver disease is understood as the loss of these functions (so LFTs, the bleeding tendency, jaundice, and encephalopathy all become derivable).
Why it matters: underpins interpreting LFTs, liver failure, cirrhosis, jaundice, hepatic drug metabolism, and the bleeding/encephalopathy of liver disease — cross-ref bilirubin metabolism + bile (the next subtabs), PK/PD (first-pass), liver failure/cirrhosis.
The Liver's Strategic Position — why it does so much
  • Dual blood supply: the portal vein (~70%, nutrient-rich blood straight from the gut) + the hepatic artery (~30%, oxygenated) → the liver is the first organ to process everything absorbed ("first-pass")
  • Hepatocytes do the metabolic work; Kupffer cells (resident macrophages) clear bacteria/debris from portal blood
The first-pass point: orally-absorbed drugs/nutrients hit the liver first → first-pass metabolism (cross-ref PK/PD — why some drugs have low oral bioavailability).

  • The liver makes almost all clotting factors (including the vitamin-K-dependent II, VII, IX, X + protein C/S)
The clinical link (high-yield): liver failure → ↓clotting factors → bleeding tendency → prolonged PT/INR → PT/INR is the best marker of synthetic liver function (and rises early, as factor VII has a short half-life); cross-ref coagulation.
The two synthetic markers: albumin (long half-life → chronic synthetic function) + PT/INR (short half-life → acute synthetic function).
Detoxification — toxins, drugs & ammonia (high-yield)
  • Drug metabolism: CYP450 (Phase I) + conjugation (Phase II) → makes drugs water-soluble for excretion (cross-ref PK/PD); the basis of hepatic drug clearance + interactions
  • Ammonia → urea (the urea cycle): gut bacteria + protein metabolism produce ammonia (neurotoxic) → the liver converts it to urea (excreted renally)
  • Hormone + bilirubin metabolism: the liver clears hormones (e.g. oestrogen — why liver failure → gynaecomastia/spider naevi) and conjugates bilirubin (cross-ref bilirubin note)
The clinical link (high-yield): liver failure → ↓ammonia clearance → ↑ammonia → hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, coma) → treated with lactulose (traps ammonia in the gut) + rifaximin (↓ammonia-producing gut bacteria).

Overview — Bilirubin Metabolism
Bilirubin is the breakdown product of haemoglobin — and tracking its journey from red cell to bile explains jaundice and how to classify its cause.
The organising principle: bilirubin passes through three stages — production (from haem) → conjugation (in the liver) → excretion (via bile/gut) — and jaundice is classified by where in this pathway the problem lies: pre-hepatic, hepatic, or post-hepatic.
Why it matters: the single framework for classifying jaundice, interpreting conjugated vs unconjugated bilirubin, Gilbert's, haemolysis, and biliary obstruction — cross-ref red cell physiology (haem breakdown), liver function, bile (next subtab), haemolytic anaemia.

Overview — Bile & the Enterohepatic Circulation
Bile is the liver's secretion that digests fat and excretes waste — and most of its components are recycled through the gut and back to the liver (the enterohepatic circulation), an efficient conservation system.
The organising principle: bile has two jobs — fat digestion (bile salts) and excretion (bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs) — and the enterohepatic circulation recycles bile salts so the body doesn't have to make them fresh each meal. Disrupting bile flow or composition causes gallstones, fat malabsorption, and cholestasis.
Why it matters: explains gallstones, fat malabsorption/steatorrhoea, bile-acid diarrhoea, the ADEK vitamins, and obstructive jaundice — cross-ref liver function + bilirubin metabolism, digestion/absorption (fat), gut hormones (CCK), gallstones.

The gallstone balance (high-yield): bile salts + phospholipids keep cholesterol dissolved; if cholesterol is in excess (or bile salts ↓) → cholesterol precipitates → gallstones.
Bile Production & Flow — made, stored, released
  • Made continuously by hepatocytes → secreted into bile canaliculi → bile ducts
  • Stored + concentrated in the gallbladder between meals (water reabsorbed → bile concentrated up to ~10×)
  • Released into the duodenum when needed: a fatty meal → CCK (cross-ref gut hormones) → gallbladder contracts + sphincter of Oddi relaxes → bile flows into the duodenum
The clinical link: a gallstone obstructing the cystic/common bile duct → biliary colic (pain when the gallbladder contracts against the obstruction, esp. after fatty meals — CCK-driven).
Bile Salts & Fat Digestion — the digestive function
  • Bile salts are amphipathic (water- and fat-soluble ends) → they emulsify fat (break large globules into small droplets → ↑surface area for lipase) and form micelles that ferry fat-breakdown products to the enterocyte (cross-ref digestion/absorption)
  • Essential for absorbing: fat + the fat-soluble vitamins ADEK
The malabsorption link: ↓bile (obstruction, cholestasis, bile-salt loss) → fat malabsorption → steatorrhoea + ADEK deficiency (cross-ref).
The Enterohepatic Circulation — the recycling system (core concept)
The principle — bile salts are too valuable to excrete
  • Bile salts released into the duodenum → emulsify fat → travel down the gut → reabsorbed in the terminal ileum → return to the liver via the portal vein → re-secreted into bile
The efficiency: the bile salt pool recirculates several times per meal; only ~5% is lost in faeces (and replaced by new hepatic synthesis) → the body conserves bile salts rather than making them fresh each time.
The terminal ileum is the key site (high-yield): bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (same site as B12 — cross-ref digestion/absorption) → so terminal ileal disease/resection (Crohn's) → bile salt malabsorption:
  • Bile salts spill into the colon → bile-acid diarrhoea (they irritate the colon) → treated with colestyramine (binds bile acids)
  • + depleted bile salt pool → fat malabsorption + ↑gallstone risk (less bile salt to keep cholesterol soluble)
Bile and Excretion — the waste-disposal function
  • Bile is the route for excreting substances the kidney can't handle: bilirubin (cross-ref), cholesterol, drugs/metabolites, copper (→ Wilson's disease if it accumulates)
The obstruction link: blocked bile flow (gallstone, tumour) → conjugated bilirubin can't be excreted → obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools — cross-ref bilirubin note) + bile salts back up → itch (pruritus).

Overview — A Differential-Diagnosis Cluster

The examined skill is taking an anorectal complaint and placing it correctly — the benign causes overlap.

CAN'T MISS: the dangerous mimics are colorectal cancer (bleeding) and Crohn's disease (fistulae / abscesses) — always exclude these.
THE TRIAGE FORK — three questions: painful or painless? · bleeding or discharge? · lump or no lump? These split the whole group:
ConditionPainBleedingDischargeLump
HaemorrhoidsPainless (unless thrombosed)Bright red, on surfaceMucusProlapsing
Anal fissureVery painful (on defecation)Bright red, small—Sentinel tag
Perianal abscessPainful, throbbing——Tender fluctuant lump
Fistula-in-anoMild / none—Persistent dischargeExternal opening
Pilonidal sinusPainful if infected—DischargeNatal cleft
The Shared Exam Approach
  • Inspection — perianal skin, prolapse, external openings, skin tags.
  • DRE — tone, masses, tenderness.
  • Proctoscopy — for haemorrhoids / fissure.
CLUE: a fissure is often too painful to examine without anaesthesia — the pain itself is diagnostic.
Two Cross-Cutting Principles
Abscess → Fistula

Fistula formation occurs through chronic infection of the anal crypt glands — an abscess forms, then discharges pus via the skin, leaving a tract. The same cryptoglandular process, acute vs chronic.

Crohn's Association

Perianal disease (esp. fistulae + abscesses) is a classic Crohn's feature — recurrent / complex / multiple perianal disease should prompt thinking about IBD.

⭐ Exam Pearls
Triage fork: painful/painless · bleeding/discharge · lump? resolves most complaints.
Haemorrhoids = painless bright-red bleeding ON the stool surface (vs cancer = mixed in); grade 1–4; band 1st/2nd, operate 3rd/4th.
Fissure = severe pain on defecation; posterior midline; topical GTN/diltiazem (lateral/multiple → Crohn's).
Abscess = painful tender fluctuant lump → drain within 24 h.
Fistula = persistent discharge, follows an abscess; Goodsall's rule; fistulotomy vs seton.
Pilonidal = young hirsute male, natal cleft, midline pits.
Ties the cluster together: abscess→fistula and Crohn's.
Always exclude colorectal cancer / IBD as the cause of any anorectal bleeding.
Overview
  • Abnormal swelling / enlargement of the anal vascular cushions (normally help the sphincter maintain continence).
  • Three cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock (lithotomy); peak age 45–65.
Internal (above dentate line)

Painless — visceral innervation; prolapse & bleed.

External (below dentate line)

Can be painful — somatic innervation.

DegreeDescription
1stRemain in the rectum
2ndProlapse on defecation, spontaneously reduce
3rdProlapse, require digital reduction
4thPersistently prolapsed
Risk Factors

Excessive straining (chronic constipation), increasing age, raised intra-abdominal pressure (pregnancy, chronic cough, ascites); also portal hypertension.

Clinical Features
  • Painless bright red rectal bleeding after defecation, on paper or covering the pan.
  • Pruritus, rectal fullness / lump, soiling.
  • Large prolapsed haemorrhoids can thrombose — very painful, acute purple/blue, oedematous, tense, tender mass.
DISCRIMINATOR: haemorrhoidal blood is on the surface of the stool / on the paper, NOT mixed in — blood mixed through the stool points to cancer.
Investigations

Proctoscopy confirms; FBC + clotting if significant bleeding / anaemia; colonoscopy to exclude concurrent pathology before surgery.

Management (conservative → outpatient → surgical)
  • Most managed conservatively: increase fibre + fluid, laxatives, topical analgesia (lignocaine gel).
  • Thrombosed: ice packs + topical lidocaine; haemorrhoidectomy usually NOT recommended.
  • 1st / 2nd degree → rubber-band ligation.
  • Surgical: HAL / THD (Doppler-guided artery ligation) for 2nd/3rd; haemorrhoidectomy for 3rd/4th (Milligan-Morgan or stapled).
  • Complications of surgery: recurrence, anal stricturing, faecal incontinence.
AVOID opioid analgesia — it worsens constipation and the underlying problem.
Overview
  • A split in the distal anal mucosa — sharp anal pain on defecation and bleeding.
  • Acute (<6 weeks) vs chronic (>6 weeks); chronic develops the triad of fissure + sentinel skin tag + hypertrophied anal papilla.
LOCATION CLUE: posterior midline in the vast majority (poorest blood supply); anterior / lateral / multiple fissures → think a secondary cause (Crohn's, malignancy, infection).
Risk Factors

Constipation / hard stool (the main one), low fibre; secondary causes — IBD, infection.

Clinical Features

Intense, sharp / tearing pain on defecation (lasts hours after), bright red bleeding (small volume, on paper); patient often too tender for DRE / proctoscopy.

Management (the conservative ladder)
  • Conservative first-line: fibre + fluids, stool softeners / laxatives, topical analgesia, sitz baths.
  • Topical GTN or diltiazem (relax the internal sphincter → improve blood flow → heal).
  • Refractory: botulinum toxin injection; lateral internal sphincterotomy (definitive but small risk of incontinence).
GTN's classic side effect = headache — a common reason for poor adherence.
Overview
  • A localised collection of pus; ~90% arise from cryptoglandular gland infection at the dentate line — when blocked, an abscess forms, particularly in the intersphincteric space.
  • Classified by location: perianal (commonest), then ischiorectal, intersphincteric, supralevator.
  • Twice as common in men.

Painful, throbbing, tender fluctuant perianal lump, erythema, ± fever / systemic upset.

If no abscess is visible and DRE isn't possible due to pain / sphincter spasm, suspect an intersphincteric abscess or anal fissure.

If an abscess is clearly present, no further investigations are required before treatment; MRI / EUA for complex / recurrent disease (to define tracts).

Surgical drainage within 24 h (RCS) — especially urgent in diabetes, systemic sepsis or immunocompromise.

Overview
  • A chronic abnormal epithelial-lined tract connecting the anorectal lumen (internal opening) to the perineal / buttock skin (external opening).

Persistent perianal discharge (pus / blood / faeculent), recurrent abscesses, an external opening on inspection ± palpable cord.

MRI pelvis (map the tract, esp. complex / Crohn's), EUA.

Fistulotomy

Lay open low / simple tracts.

For high tracts crossing significant sphincter (preserve continence) — esp. Crohn's-related fistulae.

Treat the underlying Crohn's if present.

  • A hair-containing sinus tract in the natal cleft (sacrococcygeal) — hair penetrates the skin and drives a foreign-body reaction.

Intermittent natal-cleft discharge / swelling; presents acutely as a painful pilonidal abscess; visible midline pits.

Incision + drainage.

Coeliac disease: autoimmune sensitivity to gluten → immune-mediated mucosal damage → villous atrophy + malabsorption.

💡 Strong genetic link: HLA-DQ2 (95%) and HLA-DQ8. Cross-ref autoimmune cluster: T1DM, thyroid disease, Addison's — all share HLA/autoimmune associations and cluster with coeliac.
Clinical Features
GI Symptoms
  • Chronic / intermittent diarrhoea (often steatorrhoea — pale, fatty, floating)
  • Bloating, abdominal distension, cramping
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Weight loss, failure to thrive (in children)
Malabsorption Consequences
  • Unexplained anaemia — commonest presenting clue in adults (iron ± folate ± B12)
  • Fatigue, mouth ulcers (aphthous)
  • Bone pain / fractures (Ca/vit D deficiency)
  • Subfertility
⭐ Dermatitis herpetiformis — the pathognomonic skin manifestation: intensely itchy, blistering rash on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). "Rash + diarrhoea" stem = coeliac until proven otherwise (treat with a gluten-free diet; dapsone gives rapid symptom control).
📷 Image placeholder — Dermatitis herpetiformis — clusters of intensely itchy vesicles and excoriated papules symmetrically over the extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks)
💡 Adults often present subtly or atypically — "iron-deficiency anaemia not responding to iron" or chronic fatigue. Low threshold to test serology.
Investigations
🩸
IgA tTG Antibody (First-Line)
IgA tissue transglutaminase — the first-line serology test. Always request total IgA alongside it (see traps below).
🔭
Duodenal Biopsy at OGD (Gold Standard)
Villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis + lamina propria lymphocytic infiltrate. Positive serology + positive biopsy = confirmed diagnosis. In children, ESPGHAN guidance allows a no-biopsy diagnosis if tTG-IgA is >10× the upper limit of normal with a positive endomysial antibody (EMA) on a second sample and consistent symptoms.
📷 Image placeholder — Duodenal biopsy histology in coeliac disease — subtotal villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (compared with normal finger-like villi)
🩺
Bloods
FBC (anaemia), ferritin, folate, B12, calcium, vit D, LFTs. Blood film: Howell-Jolly bodies (functional hyposplenism).
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film showing Howell-Jolly bodies — small round basophilic nuclear remnants within red cells, indicating functional hyposplenism
⭐ Two Testing Traps (Commonly Examined)
Trap 1 — Must Keep Eating Gluten

Patient must be on a gluten-containing diet for ≥6 weeks (gluten in ≥1 meal/day) before serology and biopsy. A gluten-free diet normalises antibodies and heals villi → false-negative result.

Trap 2 — IgA Deficiency

Coeliac is associated with selective IgA deficiency. If IgA is low, the IgA-tTG will be falsely negative despite active disease. Always check total IgA — if deficient, use IgG-based tests (IgG-DGP or IgG-tTG).

Management
🌾
Lifelong Gluten-Free Diet
The only curative treatment. Avoid wheat, barley, rye. Oats usually tolerated unless contaminated. Villi recover → symptoms and serology normalise. Monitor adherence with serial tTG.
💉
Pneumococcal Vaccine
Functional hyposplenism → ↑ susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria (Pneumococcus, Hib, Meningococcus). Vaccinate + 5-yearly booster (same logic as sickle cell/other asplenic states).
💊
Replace Deficiencies
Iron, folate, B12, calcium, vitamin D as indicated. Osteoporosis screening (DEXA) if prolonged untreated disease.
Complications
🩸
Malabsorption Anaemias
Iron-deficiency (↓MCV), folate deficiency (↑MCV), B12 deficiency (↑MCV + neurological). Often mixed picture. Cross-ref haematology.
🦴
Osteoporosis / Osteomalacia
Calcium + vit D malabsorption → reduced bone density. ↑ fracture risk. DEXA monitoring.
🫁
Functional Hyposplenism
Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film (nuclear remnants normally culled by the spleen). ↑ infection risk from encapsulated organisms → drives vaccination.
EATL (T-cell Lymphoma)
Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma — the key malignancy of coeliac disease. Also: small-bowel adenocarcinoma, oesophageal cancer. New B-symptoms or weight loss despite strict GFD → suspect EATL.

Mechanism: gluten → autoimmune villous atrophy → malabsorption. Genetic: HLA-DQ2 (95%) + HLA-DQ8.
IgA tTG = first-line serology; duodenal biopsy = gold standard (villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + IEL).
Testing trap 1: must eat gluten for ≥6 weeks before testing — GFD causes false negative.
Testing trap 2: check total IgA — IgA deficiency → false-negative tTG → use IgG-DGP/tTG instead.

EATL (T-cell lymphoma) = key malignancy. New B-symptoms / weight loss despite GFD → suspect it.

Overview

IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome): a functional bowel disorder — symptoms arising from abnormal gut functioning with no identifiable structural or organic disease.

The Central Fork

Step 1: Exclude organic causes (red flags + investigations)
Step 2: Diagnose positively on symptom criteria

IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion — but made positively, not just by default.

IBS Triad

Intestinal discomfort
Bowel habit change
Stool abnormality

💡 Cross-references: IBD (the organic mirror — IBS is what remains when inflammation is excluded) · Coeliac disease (key mimic — always exclude) · Colorectal cancer (the red-flag concern in any bowel habit change)
Clinical Features
🔥
Abdominal Pain
Relieved by defecation. Worse after eating. Cramping, colicky. Lower abdomen typically.
🔄
Altered Bowel Habit
Fluctuating — diarrhoea, constipation, or alternating. Urgency, straining, sensation of incomplete emptying.
💨
Bloating / Distension
Often worse after eating, relieved partially by defecation. Passage of mucus (no blood).
💡 The IBS pattern is chronic, relapsing, and without alarm features. Pain relieved by defecation + fluctuating habit without weight loss/bleeding = functional until red flags say otherwise.

IBS does NOT cause these features — any one of them mandates investigation for organic disease:

Red Flag Concern

AnaemiaCancer, coeliac, IBD

⭐ IBS does NOT cause weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, or nocturnal symptoms. Any of these = investigate for IBD, cancer, or coeliac first.
Investigations

All results should be normal in IBS — the purpose is to exclude organic mimics, not diagnose IBS itself.

🩸
FBC + CRP/ESR
Normal in IBS. Raised CRP/ESR = IBD — a key discriminator. FBC checks for anaemia (cancer, coeliac, IBD).
🧪
Faecal Calprotectin
The IBS vs IBD discriminator. Raised = mucosal inflammation (IBD). Normal = functional disorder (IBS). Highly sensitive for active colonic inflammation.
🔬

Mandatory before diagnosing IBS — coeliac is a treatable mimic with identical GI presentation. Cross-ref coeliac note.
🩺

If ovarian cancer suspected in women — bloating + abdominal symptoms overlap with IBS. Do not miss.

📋 ≥6 months of abdominal pain/discomfort that is relieved by defecation OR associated with altered stool frequency or form, PLUS ≥2 of the following:

  • Straining / urgency / incomplete emptying
  • Bloating or distension
  • Symptoms worse after eating
  • Passage of mucus
Management
Lifestyle & Diet (First)
  • Regular unhurried meals; avoid skipping; adequate fluid intake
  • Limit caffeine, alcohol, fizzy drinks
  • Adjust fibre (↑ for constipation, ↓ insoluble fibre for diarrhoea/bloating)
  • Low-FODMAP diet (dietitian-led) — fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, polyols; evidence-based intervention for refractory symptoms

Dominant Symptom First-Line Notes

Amitriptyline preferred over SSRI. Modulates gut-brain axis, reduces visceral pain and alters gut motility. Use at low dose (10–30mg nocte). Consider an SSRI if a TCA is ineffective or not tolerated (NICE).

CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy for refractory IBS. Strong evidence for psychosocial component of functional GI disease.

IBS = functional (no pathology). Diagnose positively on criteria — but only after excluding red flags and organic mimics.
IBS does NOT cause weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, or nocturnal symptoms → these mandate investigation.

Always exclude coeliac (IgA tTG) before diagnosing IBS — it is a common, treatable mimic.
Criteria: ≥6 months pain relieved by defecation / altered habit + ≥2 supporting features.
Rx by symptom: antispasmodic (pain) · ispaghula/avoid lactulose (constipation) · loperamide (diarrhoea). 2nd-line: TCA (amitriptyline).

Overview

IBD: recurrent inflammation of the GI tract. Two types: Crohn's disease and Ulcerative Colitis (UC) — distinguished by distribution, depth, and pathological pattern.

Crohn's Disease — Overview

Crohn's disease: transmural, skip-lesion inflammation affecting any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus. Terminal ileum is the commonest site. Fistulae, strictures, and abscesses are its distinctive complications.

⭐ NESTTS: Non-bloody diarrhoea · Entire GI tract · Skip lesions · Transmural · Thick wall/fistulae · Smoking worsens
Clinical Features
🔄
Diarrhoea (Non-Bloody)
Chronic/intermittent, usually non-bloody. May be steatorrhoeic if terminal ileum involvement (↓fat absorption).
⚖️
Weight Loss + Malnutrition
Malabsorption + anorexia + catabolism. Prominent feature distinguishing Crohn's from UC clinically.
🔥
Abdominal Pain
RIF pain (terminal ileum) — mimics appendicitis. Colicky, post-prandial if strictures.
🩹
Perianal Disease
Fistulae, skin tags, fissures, abscesses — pathognomonic of Crohn's. May predate GI symptoms.
👄
Mouth Ulcers
Aphthous ulcers — reflects mouth-to-anus distribution. Often the first/only sign in some patients.
Management
Induce Remission
💊
Steroids — 1st-line
Oral prednisolone (mild-moderate) · IV hydrocortisone (severe/hospitalised). Budesonide for terminal ileal/right-sided disease (topical effect, fewer systemic SE).
↓ add / steroid-sparing
🔬
Azathioprine / Mercaptopurine
Steroid-sparing immunosuppressant. Check TPMT activity before starting — TPMT deficiency → severe myelosuppression (classic prescribing SBA).
↓ refractory / fistulating
💉
Infliximab (anti-TNF)
Biologic therapy for refractory or fistulating disease. Also: adalimumab, ustekinumab, vedolizumab, and newer advanced therapies — IL-23 inhibitors (risankizumab) and JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib). Screen for TB before starting.
↓ children / steroid concern
🍶
Enteral Nutrition
Preferred over steroids in children. Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) — equivalent efficacy to steroids with nutritional benefit and no steroid SE.
Maintain Remission
1st-Line

Azathioprine / mercaptopurine — the backbone of maintenance. Methotrexate if intolerant.

2nd-Line

Methotrexate (monitor LFTs, folate supplementation). Anti-TNF biologics for persistent/severe.

Surgery (Not Curative)
  • Resect isolated/symptomatic disease (e.g. terminal ileal resection)
  • Treat strictures (balloon dilatation or stricturoplasty)
  • Perianal fistula → MRI + metronidazole ± seton + infliximab
  • Abscess → I&D + antibiotics
  • Surgery does NOT cure Crohn's — disease recurs at new sites (panenteric disease)
Complications
🔗
Fistulae
Transmural inflammation → tracks between loops (entero-enteric), bladder (enterovesical → pneumaturia), skin (enterocutaneous), perianal. Pathognomonic of Crohn's.
🚧
Strictures / Obstruction
Fibrosis from repeated transmural inflammation → luminal narrowing → Kantor's string sign on contrast. Bowel obstruction.
🫘
Gallstones
Terminal ileum disease → ↓ bile acid reabsorption → bile acid pool depleted → cholesterol gallstones.
🩸
Malabsorption / Nutritional
B12 deficiency (terminal ileum), fat-soluble vitamins, iron, folate. Oxalate renal stones.
⭐ Exam Pearls — Crohn's
Transmural + skip lesions + mouth to anus. Terminal ileum commonest site.
Non-bloody diarrhoea + weight loss (contrast: UC = bloody + mucus).
Histology: granulomas + ↑goblet cells. Endoscopy: cobblestone + deep ulcers + skip lesions.
Radiology: Kantor's string sign (stricture), rose-thorn ulcers, fistulae on contrast.
Check TPMT before azathioprine — deficiency → myelosuppression.
Smoking worsens Crohn's (opposite of UC). Perianal fistulae = pathognomonic.
Surgery not curative — panenteric disease recurs. Infliximab for fistulating/refractory.
Ulcerative Colitis — Overview

Ulcerative Colitis (UC): mucosal inflammation of the colon and rectum, continuous from the rectum upward, never extending past the ileocaecal valve. Bloody diarrhoea is the hallmark.

⭐ CLOSEUP: Continuous · Large bowel only · Only mucosa · Smoking protective · Elevated cancer risk · Ulcerations/pseudopolyps · PSC association
Clinical Features & Severity
🩸
Bloody Diarrhoea + Mucus
The hallmark. Rectal bleeding + loose stool. Tenesmus (sensation of incomplete emptying), urgency, LLQ/central cramping pain.
🔥
Systemic Upset (Severe)
Fever, tachycardia, weight loss, ↓Hb, ↑CRP/ESR, ↓albumin — Truelove-Witts severe criteria.
Severity Grading — Truelove-Witts
Severity Stools/day Systemic features
Mild<4None
Moderate4–6Minimal
Severe>6 bloodyFever, tachycardia, anaemia (Hb<10.5), ↑ESR (>30)
Management
Flare Triggers to Avoid

Stress · NSAIDs · Antibiotics · Stopping smoking (smoking is protective — cessation can precipitate a flare)

Induce Remission
Mild–Moderate
  • Aminosalicylates (mesalazine) 1st-line
  • Oral ± rectal (suppository/enema) — rectal only reaches splenic flexure; use oral if beyond left colon
  • Steroids 2nd-line (oral prednisolone)
Severe (Admit)
  • IV hydrocortisone 1st-line
  • No response by day 3–5 → IV ciclosporin or infliximab
  • LMWH (high VTE risk in active colitis)
  • Colectomy if failing medical therapy
  • AXR to exclude toxic megacolon
Maintain Remission
1st-Line — Aminosalicylates

Mesalazine oral ± rectal. Monitor FBC — aminosalicylates → agranulocytosis (check FBC if fever/sore throat — same vigilance as carbimazole) and pancreatitis.

After Severe / Frequent Relapses

Azathioprine / mercaptopurine (check TPMT). Anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, vedolizumab) for refractory; newer options include JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib), IL-23 inhibitors (ustekinumab, mirikizumab) and the S1P modulator ozanimod.

Surgery — Curative
📋 Panproctocolectomy removes the entire diseased organ → cures UC. Options:
  • Permanent ileostomy (simpler, reliable)
  • Ileoanal pouch (J-pouch) — reservoir fashioned from ileum, anastomosed to anus; avoids permanent stoma but risk of pouchitis
Complications
💥
Toxic Megacolon
Colonic dilatation >6cm on AXR + systemic toxicity. Life-threatening. Emergency colectomy if medical therapy fails within 24–48h.
📷 Image placeholder — Abdominal X-ray of toxic megacolon — marked dilatation of the transverse colon (>6 cm) with mucosal islands/thumbprinting in acute severe colitis
🦠
Colorectal Cancer
↑ Risk with pancolitis, long disease duration (>10yr), PSC. Surveillance colonoscopy every 1–5 years depending on risk.
🫀
Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)
Stricturing of biliary tree — the classic UC hepatic association. Raised ALP. ↑ cholangiocarcinoma risk. Cross-ref liver.
🩸
Anaemia
Chronic blood loss → iron-deficiency anaemia. Anaemia of chronic disease (↑IL-6, ↓erythropoiesis).
⭐ Exam Pearls — UC
Continuous mucosal inflammation from rectum upward — never past ileocaecal valve.
Bloody diarrhoea + mucus + tenesmus — the hallmark (contrast: Crohn's = non-bloody + weight loss).
Histology: crypt abscesses + goblet cell depletion. Endoscopy: pseudopolyps, continuous. Radiology: lead-pipe colon.
Smoking is PROTECTIVE in UC. Stopping smoking can precipitate a flare.
Severe flare: admit → IV hydrocortisone → ciclosporin/infliximab → LMWH → AXR (toxic megacolon).
Mild-moderate: mesalazine 1st-line. Aminosalicylates → agranulocytosis (monitor FBC).
Surgery IS curative — panproctocolectomy. J-pouch or permanent ileostomy.
Complications: toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer (↑ with pancolitis/long disease), PSC.
LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Difficile Infection:
Overview

Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) — pseudomembranous colitis caused by toxin-mediated mucosal damage after broad-spectrum antibiotics suppress normal gut flora, allowing C. diff overgrowth.

Core framing: "Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics + new diarrhoea, especially in hospital = C. diff until proven otherwise." Always exclude C. diff toxin in every IBD flare with diarrhoea before escalating immunosuppression.
Causes — The "4 Cs"
The "4 Cs" — Causative Antibiotics
  • Cephalosporins — leading cause
  • Ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolones)
  • Clindamycin
  • Co-amoxiclav
Additional Risk Factors
  • PPIs — ↓ gastric acid barrier
  • Advanced age
  • Hospitalisation / healthcare exposure
  • Immunosuppression

Mechanism: antibiotics → flora suppression → C. diff overgrows → toxin A (enterotoxin) + toxin B (cytotoxin) → mucosal damage → pseudomembranous colitis

📷 Image placeholder — Colonoscopy of pseudomembranous colitis — raised yellow-white adherent plaques (pseudomembranes) on inflamed colonic mucosa
Clinical Features
Typical Presentation
  • Profuse, foul-smelling diarrhoea
  • Diffuse abdominal pain / cramping
  • Fever
  • Raised WCC (leukocytosis)
  • Dehydration
  • Recent antibiotics / hospitalisation
Severe / Life-Threatening
  • Toxic megacolon — colon >6 cm + systemic sepsis (shared with UC)
  • Ileus (silent abdomen)
  • Perforation
  • Hypotension / shock
Imaging clue: thumbprinting (mucosal oedema) on AXR
📷 Image placeholder — Abdominal X-ray in severe C. difficile colitis — thumbprinting (thickened, oedematous haustra) and colonic dilatation of toxic megacolon (>6 cm)

Key threshold: WCC >15 or AKI = severe — escalate early.
Investigations
Diagnostic
  • Stool C. diff toxin (CDT) — gold standard; detects toxin A & B
  • GDH antigen — sensitive screening; if positive, confirm with toxin assay
Critical nuance: GDH+/toxin− = colonisation, not infection. Must detect toxin — treating colonisation is a recognised error.
Severity Markers
  • FBC — WCC (severity threshold)
  • U&E / creatinine — AKI flags severity
  • CRP — elevated in active disease
  • AXR — toxic megacolon, thumbprinting, ileus if severe
  • CT abdomen — if perforation suspected
Management
First Episode — Treatment Ladder
  • Stop the offending antibiotic (where possible)
  • 1st-line: oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days
  • 2nd-line: oral fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days
  • Severe: oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS + IV metronidazole
  • Life-threatening: above + surgical review (colectomy)
Recurrent Disease
  • Within 12 weeks → oral fidaxomicin
  • After 12 weeks → oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin
  • Multiple recurrences → Faecal Microbiota Transplant (FMT)
  • Bezlotoxumab (a monoclonal antibody against toxin B) can be added to antibiotic treatment to reduce recurrence in high-risk patients
Infection Control
  • Isolate in single room with contact precautions
  • Soap-and-water handwashing — C. diff spores resist alcohol gel
  • Dedicated toilet; PPE (gloves + apron) for all contacts
  • Antibiotic stewardship — limit the 4 Cs
Updated guideline trap: metronidazole is NO LONGER first-line. Current NICE guidance: oral vancomycin = 1st-line. Older question banks still say metronidazole — know the current answer.

  • Permanent after APR — rectum + anus removed; reversal impossible
  • Sits lower left abdomen

  • Permanent after panproctocolectomy (IBD, FAP)
  • Alternative: J-pouch (ileo-anal anastomosis) — avoids permanent stoma
Gastrostomy & Urostomy
Gastrostomy — Feeding, Not Draining
  • Artificial connection between stomach and abdominal wall
  • Delivers feed directly when oral nutrition not possible
  • PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) = fitted endoscopically
  • Indications: neurological dysphagia (stroke, MND), head/neck cancer
Urostomy — Ileal Conduit (RIF, Spouted)
  • Urine bypasses the bladder and urethra
  • Indication: after cystectomy (bladder removal)
  • 15–20 cm of ileum isolated; remaining bowel re-anastomosed
  • Ureters anastomosed to isolated ileal segment
  • Distal end brought to skin as stoma → urine drains into bag
  • Spouted — urine is irritant; sited RIF

Skin / Mechanical
  • Peristomal skin irritation (esp. ileostomy/urostomy)
  • Granulomas — raised red lumps at stoma margin
  • Parastomal hernia — bowel herniates through defect
  • Prolapse — bowel telescopes through
  • Retraction — sinks below skin (leak risk)
  • Stenosis, obstruction
Functional / Metabolic
  • High-output ileostomy → dehydration + electrolyte loss (Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺) → AKI
  • Malabsorption, nutritional deficiency
  • Constipation (colostomies)
  • Body image, depression, adjustment (psychosocial)

LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticular Disease:
Overview — The Four-Stage Spectrum

Outpouchings of colonic mucosa through weak points in the bowel wall, commonest in the sigmoid colon. A spectrum from silent pouches to life-threatening peritonitis.

📷 Image placeholder — Endoscopic view of colonic diverticulosis — multiple rounded mucosal outpouchings (diverticular openings) in the sigmoid colon
StageWhatSymptoms
DiverticulosisPouches presentAsymptomatic (incidental finding)
Diverticular diseaseSymptomatic pouchesIntermittent LIF pain, altered bowel habit
DiverticulitisInflamed / infected pouchesLIF pain + systemic upset (fever, raised CRP)
Diverticular bleedVessel erosionPainless large-volume PR bleed
Cross-references: Colorectal cancer (key differential — same demographic, always exclude); IBD (faecal calprotectin distinguishes); lower GI bleed
Pathophysiology
Why Diverticula Form
  • Low-fibre diet → harder stool → straining → ↑ intraluminal pressure
  • Ageing bowel wall loses tensile strength
  • Mucosa herniates through weak points where blood vessels penetrate the circular muscle — between the taenia coli
  • Never in the rectum — complete outer longitudinal muscle layer + no taenia coli
Why They Bleed
  • A vasa recta runs directly alongside each pouch — the same anatomical weak point
  • Erosion → painless, large-volume arterial PR bleed
  • Most common cause of significant lower GI haemorrhage in adults
Risk Factors
  • Low fibre (key modifiable), high red meat, age, obesity, smoking
  • NSAIDs / steroids — ↑ perforation risk
Diverticulitis — Acute Presentation
Clinical Features
  • LIF pain (worse on movement)
  • Fever, anorexia, nausea
  • Altered bowel habit, ± PR bleeding
  • Urinary symptoms (bladder irritation)
  • LIF tenderness ± palpable mass (abscess) on exam
  • Guarding / rebound → complicated (perforation)
Simple vs Complicated
  • Simple = inflammation only
  • Complicated = abscess, perforation, fistula, or obstruction
"Left-sided appendicitis" — same inflammatory-then-perforation logic, opposite side.
Investigations
Imaging — 1st Line
  • CT abdo-pelvis — bowel wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, abscess, free air (perforation)
  • 📷 Image placeholder — CT of acute sigmoid diverticulitis — colonic diverticula with wall thickening and surrounding pericolonic fat stranding (± abscess or extraluminal free air if perforated)
  • Erect CXR — pneumoperitoneum if perforation suspected
NEVER colonoscopy acutely — perforation risk. Scope after resolution (6–8 wks) to exclude colorectal cancer.
Bloods
  • FBC — raised WCC
  • CRP — elevated; guides severity
  • U&E — AKI in sepsis
  • G&S — if surgical intervention possible
  • Faecal calprotectin — if IBD unclear
  • Urine dip — leucocytes ± haematuria from bladder irritation
Hinchey Classification → Management
StageFindingManagement
0 / IaMild / pericolic phlegmonOral antibiotics (outpatient)
Ib / IIPericolic or pelvic abscessIV antibiotics ± CT-guided drainage (>5 cm)
IIIPurulent peritonitisSurgery — Hartmann's procedure
IVFaecal peritonitisSurgery — Hartmann's procedure
Uncomplicated — Outpatient
  • Oral co-amoxiclav ≥5 days (cipro + metronidazole if pen-allergic) — but antibiotics are not routinely needed in uncomplicated diverticulitis if the patient is systemically well (NICE NG147); reserve them for systemic upset, immunosuppression or significant comorbidity
  • Paracetamol — avoid NSAIDs (↑ perforation) and opioids (mask symptoms)
  • Clear fluids, rest, review at 48h
  • Colonoscopy 6–8 weeks post-resolution to exclude CRC
Complicated — Admit
  • NBM, IV fluids, analgesia
  • IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or pip-tazo)
  • Abscess >5 cm → CT-guided drainage
  • Perforation / peritonitis → Hartmann's (sigmoid colectomy + end colostomy; ~50% reversible)
Diverticular Bleed vs Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis — Inflammatory
  • LIF pain + fever
  • Raised WCC/CRP
  • ± minor PR bleeding
Diverticular Bleed — Vascular
  • Painless, large-volume, fresh PR bleed
  • No fever, no inflammatory response
  • Usually self-limiting (80%)
Bleed management: Resuscitate → CT angiography (1st-line) → endoscopic haemostasis / embolisation → surgery if refractory
Complications
Acute
  • Abscess (CT-guided drainage if >5 cm)
  • Perforation → peritonitis → Hartmann's
  • Haemorrhage
Chronic (Fistulae)
  • Colovesical (commonest in men) → pneumaturia, faecaluria, recurrent UTIs
  • Colovaginal → faeces/flatus per vagina
  • Stricture → large bowel obstruction
  • All fistulae require surgery

Overview — Acute vs Chronic

Inadequate blood flow through mesenteric vessels → bowel ischaemia. The decisive fork: chronic (atherosclerotic, "intestinal angina") vs acute (sudden occlusion, surgical emergency).

Chronic Mesenteric Ischaemia
Classic Triad
  • Postprandial central colicky pain (~30 min after eating)
  • Weight loss (food avoidance + malabsorption)
  • Abdominal bruit
Classic exam point: ≥2 of the 3 vessels must be significantly stenosed before symptoms appear — collateral supply compensates.
Investigations & Management
  • Routine bloods often normal; check CV risk profile
  • CT angiography — diagnostic test of choice
  • Modify CV risk factors (smoking, DM, HTN)
  • Statin + antiplatelet (secondary prevention)
  • Endovascular 1st-line: percutaneous mesenteric angioplasty + stenting
  • Open surgery (endarterectomy / bypass) if endovascular fails
Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia — Surgical Emergency
SubtypeMechanismDistinguishing clue
Embolic (commonest)Clot from elsewhere lodges in SMAAF, recent MI; sudden onset, no prior Hx
ThromboticAcute-on-chronic atherosclerosis of SMAPreceding chronic mesenteric ischaemia Hx
Non-occlusive (NOMI)Low-flow state — no physical clotShock, sepsis, heart failure, vasopressors
Venous (MVT)Mesenteric vein thrombosisYounger patient, thrombophilia, slower onset
Clinical Features
  • Acute pain — out of proportion to examination findings (cardinal clue)
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Progresses to shock, peritonitis, sepsis
  • Look for embolic source: AF, valve disease
Investigations
  • FBC, U&E, clotting, amylase, LFT
  • ABG: metabolic acidosis + raised lactate — marker of ischaemic tissue
  • CT angiography — definitive; vessel occlusion ± bowel changes
📷 Image placeholder — CT angiogram of acute mesenteric ischaemia — an abrupt filling defect/occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery, with bowel-wall non-enhancement or pneumatosis if infarcted
Management
  • IV resuscitation
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (faecal contamination risk)
  • Emergency surgery: (1) resect necrotic bowel; (2) revascularise (thrombectomy/embolectomy); endovascular revascularisation (catheter thrombectomy/thrombolysis/stenting) is an option in selected patients without peritonitis or frank necrosis
  • Second-look laparotomy at 24–48h to reassess bowel viability
High mortality (~60–80%) if bowel necrosis occurs. Early CT and urgent surgery is essential.
Ischaemic Colitis — The Third Entity
What It Is
  • Acute, transient compromise of blood flow to large bowel (not small bowel)
  • Watershed areas: splenic flexure (SMA/IMA border) and rectosigmoid junction (IMA/internal iliac)
  • Usually self-limiting; rarely progresses to necrosis
Features, Ix & Mx
  • Lower-left abdominal pain + bloody diarrhoea
  • CT / AXR: thumbprinting (mucosal oedema)
  • Colonoscopy confirms
  • Management: conservative — IV fluids, antibiotics, bowel rest; surgery only for gangrene/perforation/stricture
The contrast: Acute mesenteric ischaemia = SMA, small bowel, catastrophic, emergency surgery. Ischaemic colitis = IMA/watershed, large bowel, usually self-limiting, conservative.
